quick_notes.title: Average Basics
quick_notes.detail: Average : Sum/Total. Average of AP : (First + Last)/2.
quick_notes.explanation: An average is a single number that represents a group of numbers. To find a simple average, you add up all the numbers in the group, which is called the sum, and then divide that sum by the total count of numbers in the group. For example, the average of the numbers 2, 4, and 6 is found by adding them to get a sum of 12, then dividing 12 by 3 (the total count of numbers), which gives an average of 4. There is a special shortcut for finding the average of numbers that are in an Arithmetic Progression, or AP, which is a list of numbers where each number increases by the same fixed amount, like 2, 4, 6, 8. For an AP, the average is simply the first number plus the last number, then divided by 2. So for the AP 2, 4, 6, 8, the average is (2 plus 8) divided by 2, which equals 5.

quick_notes.title: Average of First n Naturals
quick_notes.detail: (n+1)/2. Average of first n Odd : n. Average of first n Even : n+1.
quick_notes.explanation: The average of the first n natural numbers, where natural numbers are the counting numbers starting from 1 (like 1, 2, 3, ... up to n), is calculated by adding 1 to n and then dividing by 2, written as (n+1)/2. For example, the first 5 natural numbers are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; their sum is 15, and dividing by 5 gives an average of 3, which matches (5+1)/2 = 3. The average of the first n odd numbers, which are numbers like 1, 3, 5, 7, ... (each odd number is one more than an even number), equals n itself, so for the first 3 odd numbers (1, 3, 5) the average is 3. The average of the first n even numbers, which are numbers like 2, 4, 6, 8, ... (each even number is a multiple of 2), equals n+1, so for the first 3 even numbers (2, 4, 6) the average is 4.

quick_notes.title: Time and Work (LCM Method)
quick_notes.detail: Total Work : LCM of individual times. Efficiency : Work / Time.
quick_notes.explanation: Title: Time and Work (LCM Method) In time and work problems, we first find the total work by taking the Least Common Multiple, or LCM, of the individual times each person takes to finish the job. For example, if person A takes 4 days and person B takes 6 days to complete the same work alone, the LCM of 4 and 6 is 12, so we say the total work is 12 units. Next, we calculate each person's efficiency, which means how much work they do in one day, by dividing the total work by their time: for A, efficiency is 12 divided by 4 equals 3 units per day, and for B, it is 12 divided by 6 equals 2 units per day. To find how long they take working together, we add their efficiencies: 3 plus 2 equals 5 units per day, then divide the total work by that combined efficiency: 12 divided by 5 equals 2.4 days. This method works for any number of workers, as long as you first find the LCM of all their individual times to get a common total work amount. Remember, the LCM is the smallest number that is a multiple of each given time, and efficiency is always work done per unit of time.

quick_notes.title: Efficiency Rule
quick_notes.detail: A:B Efficiency 2:3 -> Time 3:2. (e.g., A is twice as fast as B).
quick_notes.explanation: This rule helps you compare how fast two people or machines do the same work. The word "efficiency" here means the speed or rate at which work is completed. If A and B have an efficiency ratio of 2 to 3, that means for every 2 units of work A does in a given time, B does 3 units of work in the same time. Because B is more efficient, B takes less time to finish the same amount of work. The time ratio is the opposite of the efficiency ratio, so if the efficiency ratio is 2:3, the time ratio for completing the same job is 3:2. For example, if A is twice as fast as B, meaning A has an efficiency of 2 and B has an efficiency of 1, then the time A takes is half the time B takes.

quick_notes.title: Combined Work
quick_notes.detail: Time (A+B) : (A * B) / (A + B). (Shortcut for two people).
quick_notes.explanation: This lesson is about a simple way to calculate how long two people take to finish a job when they work together. Imagine two people, A and B. Let the time A takes to do the whole job alone be called A, and the time B takes to do the whole job alone be called B. The time it takes for both of them to complete the same job when they work together is found using this formula: multiply A and B, then divide that result by A plus B. As an example, if A alone takes 2 hours to paint a room, and B alone takes 3 hours, then the combined time is (2 times 3) divided by (2 plus 3), which is 6 divided by 5, or 1.2 hours. This shortcut only works for exactly two people working on the same task at the same time.
